title: Defining a default parameter to use when the argument is omitted for `name='user'`
reading_goal: Read the structure where the ``name='user'`` in the function definition specifies the default value to use when the `name` parameter is omitted in the call.
question: What does `name="user"` mean?
choices: If the name argument is omitted, "user" is used.
answer: If the name argument is omitted, "user" is used.
explanation: 1) Check the parameter name in the function definition parentheses. 2) The default value on the right side of the equals sign is the string "user." 3) The call to `greet()` does not include an argument for `name`. 4) Therefore, the default value "user" is bound to `name`.
project_context: This relates to understanding the default behavior of functions and CLI helpers with optional parameters.
reading_goal_internal: 함수 정의 괄호의 `name='user'`가 호출에서 name 값을 주지 않았을 때 사용할 기본값을 지정한다는 구조를 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A default parameter is defined in the form ``parameter=default_value``, and if that argument is omitted when the function is called, its default value is used.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Separate the parameter name from the default value on the right side of the equals sign, then check if there is an argument corresponding to the actual call.
concept_explanation.key_point: Default expressions are evaluated when a function is defined. While strings are immutable and therefore pose no obvious risk of sharing, care must be taken with mutable defaults.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that defaults are always created as new objects each time they are called.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the `kind` argument is omitted, the default string `unknown` is used.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Check the parameter name in the function definition parentheses. 2) The default value on the right side of the equals sign is the string "user." 3) The call to `greet()` does not include an argument for `name`. 4) Therefore, the default value "user" is bound to `name`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Default-parameter syntax uses the value written in the definition when the caller omits the corresponding argument.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: If the caller provides a value, such as `greet('Mina')`, that argument is used instead of the default value.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to assume that defaults are always created as new objects each time they are called.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A "default parameter" is interpreted as **the default value in the definition → whether an argument is provided during the call → the default value is used if omitted**.

title: Reading about the risks of sharing mutable default values in `def add_item(..., items=[])`
reading_goal: In the function definition header, it states that a mutable list literal is initialized once with a default value, and that multiple calls with omitted arguments can reuse the same object.
code:
def add_item(x, items=[]):
    items.append(x)
    return items

first = add_item("a")
second = add_item("b")
print(second)
question: What is the most important point to keep in mind when defining the `target` function?
choices: A default list can be shared between calls.
The function name has no underscore.
answer: A default list can be shared between calls.
explanation: 1) When the function is defined, a default list object named `items` is created. 2) In the first call, `items` is omitted, so that list is used, and `a` is appended to it. 3) The default object itself remains modified. 4) If `items` is omitted in the second call as well, `b` can be added to the same list.
project_context: This relates to diagnosing a bug in a helper function where results accumulate for unknown reasons.
reading_goal_internal: 함수 정의 헤더에서 mutable list literal이 default 값으로 한 번 준비되고 인자를 생략한 여러 호출이 같은 객체를 재사용할 수 있음을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `def` The header defines the function name, parameters, and defaults. Default expressions are evaluated at the time of definition.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check whether the default value is a mutable object such as a list, dict, or set, and track whether that parameter is consistently omitted in calls.
concept_explanation.key_point: If the first call to `add_item('a')` changes the default list to `['a']`, the second call can also use that same list.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to think that the line ``items=[]`` is re-executed every time a function is called, creating a new empty list.

teaching_example.code:
def remember(value, box=[]):
    box.append(value)
    return box
print(remember(1))
print(remember(2))
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the `default list` is shared between calls, the first value remains in the second result.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) When the function is defined, a default list object named `items` is created. 2) In the first call, `items` is omitted, so that list is used, and `a` is appended to it. 3) The default object itself remains modified. 4) If `items` is omitted in the second call as well, `b` can be added to the same list.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Mutable default objects are evaluated once at the time of definition and can be reused in subsequent implicit calls.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This function has an explicit ``return items``, which returns the current list.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It’s easy to think that the line ``items=[]`` is re-executed every time a function is called, creating a new empty list.

answer_explanation.takeaway: When reviewing a function definition, check the **data type of the default value → whether it is mutable → whether it can be reused between calls**.

title: Modifying the contents of an existing list object using the `items.append('a')` call
reading_goal: The item to the left of the dot currently points to an empty list, and the append method tracks the state change of adding the string “a” to the end of that object.
question: What are the values of `items` after calling `target`?
explanation: 1) `items` refers to an empty list object. 2) The `append` call operates on that existing list. 3) The string `a` is added as a single item to the end of the list. 4) If you read `items` again, it is `['a']`.
project_context: This connects to the key mutation behavior necessary to understand why the "mutable default" issue accumulates across calls.
reading_goal_internal: 점 왼쪽 items가 현재 빈 list를 가리키고 append method가 그 같은 객체 끝에 문자열 a를 추가하는 상태 변화를 추적한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `list.append(value)` is a method call that adds `value` as a single item to the end of an existing list object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Write down the state of the list before the call, and then write down the state of the same object after the call, with one argument appended to the end.
concept_explanation.key_point: The primary effect of `append` is to mutate the existing list; you should not think of the return value as a new list.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to misinterpret this as meaning that `append` automatically modifies the `items` by returning a new list, or that the original list remains unchanged.

teaching_example.walkthrough: The existing empty list object is mutated directly and becomes `[3]`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `items` refers to an empty list object. 2) The `append` call operates on that existing list. 3) The string `a` is added as a single item to the end of the list. 4) If you read `items` again, it is `['a']`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because `append` directly modified the existing list object pointed to by `items`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That value represents the state before the `append` operation is executed; after the mutation, an `a` item is added.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to misinterpret this as meaning that `append` automatically modifies the `items` by returning a new list, or that the original list remains unchanged.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A mutable method tracks the **object before the call → method execution → the modified state of the same object**.

title: Read the guard that creates a new list only when `items` is `None`.
reading_goal: Read the flow where the `if` condition evaluates to `True` in a call that receives the default value `None`, causing a new empty list to be created on every call.
code:
def add_item(x, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(x)
    return items

first = add_item("a")
second = add_item("b")
print(first, second)
question: Which output is correct after two calls that omit the argument?
explanation: 1) In the first call, the default value of `items` is `None`. 2) Since `if items is None:` evaluates to True, a new list `[]` is created, `a` is added, and `['a']` is returned. 3) The second call also starts with `items` set to `None` and creates a separate new list. 4) It returns `['b']`, with only `b` added, so the two results are not cumulative.
project_context: Help learners understand, through the code execution flow, why `items=[]` is used instead of `items=None` in real-world project functions.
reading_goal_internal: 기본값 None이 들어온 호출에서 if 조건이 True가 되어 매 호출마다 새 빈 리스트가 만들어지는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `if condition:` This is a compound statement that executes the indented block only when the condition is True.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: First, check whether the current value of `items` is `None`, and if it is `True`, trace whether `items = []` is executed.
concept_explanation.key_point: The two calls with omitted arguments each create a different new list within the function.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `items=None` It’s easy to think that, like ``items=[]``, a single mutable object is shared between calls.

teaching_example.walkthrough: In both calls, `items` starts as `None` and creates a new list within each call.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) In the first call, the default value of `items` is `None`. 2) Since `if items is None:` evaluates to True, a new list `[]` is created, `a` is added, and `['a']` is returned. 3) The second call also starts with `items` set to `None` and creates a separate new list. 4) It returns `['b']`, with only `b` added, so the two results are not cumulative.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Because a `None` sentinel is used to create a new list inside each call that omits the argument, the first and second results are not shared.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This cumulative effect can be observed in the mutable-default pattern, where an empty list is directly used as the default argument.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between the default value `None` and the point at which a list is created within a function.

answer_explanation.takeaway: Read a `None` guard as **check the current value → if it is None, create a new mutable object → perform the subsequent operation**.

title: Checking equality with a None object using `items is None`
reading_goal: Check whether the variable `items` currently points to a `None` object using ``is``, and read the resulting Boolean value.
code:
items = None
missing = items is None
print(missing)
question: What is the result of `items is None`?
explanation: 1) The current value of `items` is `None`. 2) The expression on the right is also a `None` object in Python. 3) `is` checks whether the objects in the two expressions are identical. 4) Since they are the same `None` object, the result is `True`.
project_context: This relates to the function pattern where `None` is used as a "no value provided" sentinel in optional arguments.
reading_goal_internal: 이름 items가 현재 None 객체를 가리키는지 `is`로 확인하고 그 결과 Boolean을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `is` is an identity test that checks whether two expressions point to the same object.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the current value of the name on the left and the `None` singleton on the right, then determine whether they are the same object.
concept_explanation.key_point: If `items` is None, `items is None` is True.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: `is` It is easy to think of this as an operation that is exactly the same as a standard value comparison (`==`).

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `value` points to a `None` object, the identity test returns `True`.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) The current value of `items` is `None`. 2) The expression on the right is also a `None` object in Python. 3) `is` checks whether the objects in the two expressions are identical. 4) Since they are the same `None` object, the result is `True`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: Since `items` actually points to `None`, the identity test returns `True`.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The result of a comparison expression is a Boolean, not the operands themselves.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Distinguish between the value before the comparison and the result produced by the comparison expression.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The identity test is read in the following order: **left object → right object → whether they are the same object → Boolean**.

title: Interpreting ``cache={}`` as a default parameter in a function definition
reading_goal: `cache={}` This syntax defines a default value to be used if the value is omitted when the function is called, and the flow indicates that an empty dict object is prepared at the time of definition.
code:
def remember(key, value, cache={}):
    cache[key] = value
    return cache

first = remember("a", 1)
second = remember("b", 2)
print(first is second, second)
question: `cache={}` Which of the following is the most accurate description of [this]?
choices: Define an empty dict object as the default value for `cache`.
Always create a new dict on every call.
Convert the cache to a string
Ensure that the `cache` argument is always passed.
answer: Define an empty dict object as the default value for `cache`.
explanation: 1) Verify that ``def remember(..., cache={}):`` is inside the parentheses of `def`. 2) `cache` is the parameter name, and ``{}`` is the default value expression. 3) A default dict object is prepared when the function is defined. 4) Calls that omit arguments can reuse that default object.
project_context: This serves as the foundation for understanding why the `cache` and `options` dictionaries are not set directly to their default values but instead use the `None` sentinel.
reading_goal_internal: `cache={}`가 호출 때 값을 생략하면 사용할 기본값을 정의하는 문법이며 빈 dict 객체가 정의 시점에 준비된다는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The `default parameter` specifies the default value to be used when an argument is omitted in a function definition, as in ``name=value``.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Unlike keyword arguments in function calls, first verify whether they are inside the `def` brackets, and separate parameter names from default value expressions.
concept_explanation.key_point: If you directly set a mutable dict as the default value, the same default object may be reused across multiple calls.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that an empty dict is automatically recreated every time it is called.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Since the value is omitted in the call, the string `item` specified in the definition is used as the default value.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Verify that ``def remember(..., cache={}):`` is inside the parentheses of `def`. 2) `cache` is the parameter name, and ``{}`` is the default value expression. 3) A default dict object is prepared when the function is defined. 4) Calls that omit arguments can reuse that default object.
answer_explanation.why_correct: The `cache={}` in the `def` header is a definition of a default parameter with a dictionary as its default value.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Always create a new dict on every call.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Default expressions are not re-evaluated for each omitted call.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Let’s distinguish between when default values are evaluated and when the function body is executed.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The "default parameter" is interpreted as **check the `def` location → parameter name → default value → reuse in an omitted call**.

title: `cache=None`: Create a new dictionary after the default value
reading_goal: Read the safe pattern that avoids a mutable default value by accepting `None` and creating a new dict on each call.
question: Why is the pattern of creating `cache=None` inside a function after `{}` safer than the default `cache={}`?
choices: By creating a new dictionary for each call where arguments are omitted, you can avoid sharing state between calls, so
Because `None` is automatically converted into a dict in Python.
Since a `dict` cannot be passed as a function argument,
If you set the default value to None, the function will execute only once, so
answer: By creating a new dictionary for each call where arguments are omitted, you can avoid sharing state between calls, so
explanation: 1) If the `cache` argument is omitted, it starts as `None`. 2) A new dictionary is created in `if cache is None`. 3) A new dictionary is created again in the next omitted call. 4) Therefore, items from the previous call do not mix with those of the next call. This explanation interprets the Python target on this card in the context of legacy/domain purposes, noting that creating a new dict for each call with an omitted argument prevents state sharing between calls. Common Misconception: Since `None` is automatically converted to a dictionary in Python, this option focuses only on specific syntax or context within the code and misses the card’s core meaning. Point of Misinterpretation: If you look only at the result of a single call, there is no apparent difference from `cache={}`, making it easy to overlook the sharing issue with mutable defaults. Mutable defaults avoid sharing by following the pattern: **None default → creation of a new object within the function**.
project_context: This is the context for reading practical function patterns that avoid sharing mutable default values, such as `options=None, cache=None`.
reading_goal_internal: mutable 기본값을 직접 두지 않고 None을 받은 뒤 호출마다 새 dict를 만드는 안전 패턴을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: Default parameters are a syntax feature where the value to use is specified in the function definition when the argument is omitted during a call. ``cache=None`` first accepts `None` when `cache` is omitted.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: If there is no cache for the call, ``cache`` is set to `None`, and the function body is entered. Next, since ``if cache is None:`` is `True`, ``cache = {}`` is executed.
concept_explanation.key_point: The key point is not the first output value, but that **a new mutable object is created for each call to avoid shared state**.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: If you look only at the result of a single call, there is no apparent difference from `cache={}`, so it is easy to overlook the sharing issue with mutable defaults.

teaching_example.walkthrough: If `items` is omitted, the initial value is `None`, but since a new list is created inside the function and `3` is appended to it, the function returns ``[3]``.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) If the `cache` argument is omitted, it starts with `None`. 2) A new dictionary is created at ``if cache is None``. 3) A new dictionary is created again in the next omitted call. 4) Therefore, items from the previous call do not get mixed into the next call.
answer_explanation.why_correct: "By creating a new dict for each call where arguments are omitted, you can avoid sharing state between calls" is an explanation that interprets the Python target on this card in relation to legacy/domain purposes.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Because `None` is automatically converted into a dict in Python.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This option focuses only on certain aspects of the code’s syntax or context and misses the core meaning of the card.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: If you look only at the result of a single call, there is no apparent difference from `cache={}`, so it is easy to overlook the sharing issue with mutable defaults.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The **mutable** default is **None** → the pattern of **creating a new object inside a function** avoids sharing.

title: If you change the received list to ``append()``, it will be visible to the caller as well.
reading_goal: Distinguish between the passing of mutable objects and the issue of sharing mutable defaults, and understand that changes to the same passed object are visible to the caller.
code:
def add_item(x, items):
    items.append(x)
    return items

my_items = []
add_item("a", my_items)
print(my_items)
question: `add_item("a", my_items)` Which of the following is the most appropriate explanation of how code passes mutable objects to a function?
choices: It is possible to pass a list as an argument, and if the function calls `append`, the caller’s list is also modified.
Since lists are automatically copied when passed as function arguments, the caller’s values remain unchanged.
Mutable objects must never be passed as function arguments under any circumstances.
The issue lies in the act of passing arguments itself and has nothing to do with mutable default values.
answer: It is possible to pass a list as an argument, and if the function calls `append`, the caller’s list is also modified.
explanation: 1) `my_items` and the function’s `items` refer to the same list. 2) `append` modifies that list. 3) therefore, the change is visible in the caller as well. 4) This is separate from the issue of mutable default sharing. Passing a list as an argument is possible in itself; this explanation interprets the Python target of this card—that when a function calls `append`, the same list in the caller is also modified—by connecting it to legacy/domain objectives. Common Misconception: Since lists are automatically copied when passed as function arguments, the caller’s value remains unchanged. This option focuses only on specific syntax or context in the code and misses the card’s core meaning. Point of Misinterpretation: It’s easy to calculate only the result of `append` and generalize it to “you must not pass mutable arguments.” Mutable arguments can be used. However, you must consider **whether the function modifies the same object** and **whether the default value is shared** separately.
project_context: When reading code that updates state by passing a list or dict to a function, it is necessary to distinguish between the issue of shared default values and standard parameter passing.
reading_goal_internal: mutable 객체 전달 자체와 mutable 기본값 공유 문제를 구분하고, 전달된 같은 객체의 변경이 호출자에게 보임을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `append()` is a method that adds a value to the end of a list and modifies the list itself.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: When a list is passed to a function, first consider whether the list created by the caller and the parameter inside the function point to the same object. When `append()` is executed in that state, the contents of that object are modified.
concept_explanation.key_point: **Passing a mutable object as an argument** and **sharing a mutable object as the default value in a function definition** are two different matters.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to generalize this by calculating only the `append` result and stating, “You must not pass mutable arguments.”

teaching_example.code:
def mark(tags):
    tags.append("done")

labels = []
mark(labels)
print(labels)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Since `tags.append("done")` directly modifies the list it receives, `labels` becomes `['done']` after the function call.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) `my_items` and the function’s `items` refer to the same list. 2) `append` modifies that list. 3) Therefore, the changes are visible to the caller as well. 4) This is separate from the issue of mutable default sharing.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This explanation interprets the Python target on this card—which states that passing a list as an argument is possible, and that when a function calls `append`, the caller’s list is also modified—by linking it to legacy/domain objectives.

common_wrong_choice.choice: Since lists are automatically copied when passed as function arguments, the caller’s values remain unchanged.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: This option focuses only on certain aspects of the code’s syntax or context and misses the core meaning of the card.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: It is easy to generalize this by calculating only the `append` result and stating, “You must not pass mutable arguments.”

answer_explanation.takeaway: Mutable arguments can be used. However, we consider separately whether **the function modifies the same object** and **whether default values are shared**.
